Financial planning · Performance-fee arithmetic · Visual planning guide

The same performance-fee percentage can charge differently while an investment recovers a loss

Compare an invented annual positive-gain fee with a prior-net-high-water-mark rule, trace the charges through a loss and recovery, and reconcile fees with the ending account-value difference.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hold gross returns fixed and compare two invented annual fee rules

Interactive planning lab

Ending value: annual positive-gain fee$111,974.4
Ending value: fee above the prior net high-water mark$116,640
High-water-mark ending value less annual-reset value$4,665.6

Original hypothetical four-year comparison. All paths receive the same entered gross total-return percentages with no contributions or withdrawals. One path has no modeled fees. The annual-reset path charges the selected fraction of each positive annual dollar gain, with no carryforward of past losses. The high-water-mark path charges only on gross year-end value above its prior highest post-fee year-end balance, starting at initial capital. After charging, its mark is the larger of the old mark and the new net balance. Fees crystallize once per year and are deducted inside each account; no outside fee cash is added. These are explicitly invented rules, not a description or quote for a specific fund. Management fees, hurdles, benchmarks, subscriptions, redemptions, equalization, tax and other costs are excluded. No high-water mark guarantees principal or prevents losses. Future return effects on earlier fee deductions may be positive or negative.

The central idea

The fee percentage is only one term. The eligible gain, loss carryforward, measurement dates and treatment of cash flows determine what is actually charged.

01

Ask which gain the fee percentage applies to

A statement that a manager charges a percentage of performance is incomplete without a definition of performance. A positive gain during one accounting period can occur while an investor is still recovering a loss from an earlier period.

The SEC’s investor-education page on hedge funds notes that performance fees can be subject to measures such as high-water marks and hurdle rates. That general context does not establish the terms of a particular investment, and this guide does not import the page’s US eligibility or regulatory provisions.

The tool compares two explicitly invented annual rules. One charges the selected fraction of each positive annual dollar gain. The other charges only on value above its own previous highest post-fee year-end balance. Each rule is applied to a separate account with the same initial money and gross percentage returns. A third, fee-free calculation provides a comparison point.

02

A 25% rise after a 20% fall recovers the original amount before fees

The default begins with CAD 100,000. A 20% loss leaves CAD 80,000 after the first year, and neither invented rule charges a performance fee on that negative year. The second year’s 25% gross gain is CAD 20,000, bringing gross account value back to CAD 100,000.

The annual positive-gain rule charges 20% of that second-year CAD 20,000 gain, or CAD 4,000. Its account ends at CAD 96,000. That fee is consistent with the invented annual rule even though the investor has not recovered the initial capital after fees. The first year’s loss does not carry forward under that rule.

The alternative account has a prior high-water mark of CAD 100,000. Its second-year gross value has reached that mark but has not exceeded it. Its eligible gain is therefore zero, its fee is zero and its ending balance remains CAD 100,000. The distinction comes from the gain definition, rather than a different stated fee percentage or a different market return.

03

Specify whether the high-water mark is measured before or after fees

This model starts the mark at initial capital and retains the highest post-fee year-end account value. The mark never moves downward after a loss. When an account exceeds its old mark before the annual charge, the fee applies to that excess; the next mark is the greater of the old mark and the resulting net balance.

In year three, the default mark-rule account grows from CAD 100,000 to CAD 110,000 before fees. Its CAD 10,000 excess produces a CAD 2,000 charge, leaving CAD 108,000. That becomes its new mark. In year four, a further 10% gross return produces CAD 118,800 before fees. The CAD 10,800 excess gives a CAD 2,160 fee and CAD 116,640 of ending value.

These conventions are part of the invented rule. Actual agreements can specify a different reference value, crystallization date, hurdle, benchmark or loss-recovery treatment. The tool has no new subscriptions or withdrawals, so it does not calculate how those flows would adjust a mark or allocate fees among investors.

04

A later fee can be larger when the account has retained more capital

The annual-reset account begins year three with CAD 96,000, rather than CAD 100,000. Its 10% gross gain is CAD 9,600 and its fee is CAD 1,920, leaving CAD 103,680. Year four then ends at CAD 111,974.40 after another positive-gain charge.

The mark-rule account finishes at CAD 116,640, or CAD 4,665.60 more. Its total deducted performance fees are CAD 4,160, compared with CAD 7,993.60 for the annual-reset account. Both account paths still experienced the same four gross percentage returns.

In year four alone, however, the mark-rule fee of CAD 2,160 exceeds the annual-reset fee of CAD 2,073.60. That does not contradict the earlier loss-recovery protection. The mark-rule account retained more capital and consequently generated a larger later dollar gain. Compare each eligible base and the complete path, rather than assuming that one fee rule must produce a smaller dollar charge in every single year.

05

Reconcile deducted fees with their later return effects

Without either modeled fee, the same gross-return sequence ends at CAD 121,000. The mark-rule account is CAD 4,360 below it, even though only CAD 4,160 was deducted as fees. The additional CAD 200 comes from the later return that the year-three CAD 2,000 fee would otherwise have participated in.

The waterfall adds the actual mark-rule fees and then the subsequent return effect. It does not label that last step as another charge made by the manager. It is a comparison with the counterfactual account that kept those dollars invested.

Later returns can also be negative. Removing money as a fee before a subsequent loss means those removed dollars no longer experience that loss. In such a scenario, the subsequent-return step can be negative and the ending gap smaller than total deducted fees. This accounting effect does not turn fees into income or make a charge disappear. It explains why adding fee receipts alone does not always reproduce the final account-value difference.

06

Read the loss-and-recovery grid as a contract illustration

The matrix changes the first-year loss and second-year recovery while retaining initial capital, the selected fee percentage and the last two annual returns. Each cell compares the two fee-paying accounts at the end of year four. It is a collection of assumed paths, rather than a probability distribution or an estimate of an actual manager’s performance.

A high-water mark is not principal protection. The mark-rule account can remain below the original investment for years, with no assurance of recovery. A fee-free counterfactual likewise supplies no available product or promised gross return. The illustration isolates these two fee rules while excluding management fees, trading costs, taxes and other charges.

For a real comparison, identify the fee’s eligible gain and reference period, then read how the agreement handles previous losses and external cash flows. An advertised percentage cannot answer those questions by itself. Keep the fee calculation beside the gross-return path and the actual net account value, so a recovery, a new contribution and an earned investment profit are not described as the same thing.
